article_title: Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools
citation: Melissa E. DeRosier, Ashley B. Craig, and Rebecca P. Sanchez. (2012). Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools. Advances in Human-Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1155/2012/654791
title: Zoo U: a single-player point-and-click game assessing six social skills in school-like scenes
description: Zoo U is a single-player point-and-click problem-solving game set in a school-like setting with teacher and student NPCs and zoo animals. Subject matter experts used educational and developmental psychology theories to develop six independent social scenes assessing "emotion regulation, impulse control, communication, empathy, cooperation, and initiation." Each scene scores a composite performance index computed from parsed log files, combining dialogue-choice quality, time spent on appropriate versus off-task problem solving, and the ratio of on-task to off-task behaviors.
requirements: Scene content developed by subject matter experts to elicit measurable player behaviors and dialogue choices integral to the assessed social skill
Computer logs tracking the location and time of each mouse click
constraints: Students' scores decline if they diverge too far from on-task behavior; each scene varies in emphasis on NPC interaction versus environment interaction
target_learners: third- and fourth-grade students in regular classrooms
target_learning_goals: assessment of children's social skills aptitude across six social competencies
examples: In the impulse control scene, players must ignore red-herring food crates and read the clipboard feeding instructions to score highly
key_sources: Melissa E. DeRosier, Ashley B. Craig, and Rebecca P. Sanchez. (2012). Zoo U: A Stealth Approach to Social Skills Assessment in Schools. Advances in Human-Computer Interaction. https://doi.org/10.1155/2012/654791

article_title: The critical, relational practice of instructional design in higher education: an emerging model of change agency
citation: The Critical, Relational Practice of Instructional Design in Higher Education: An Emerging Model of Change Agency. (2007).
title: Zone of moral coherence as the alignment condition for agentic instructional design practice
description: The article contends instructional design should be understood as a moral practice and proposes a zone of moral coherence: when the values of designers, clients, institutions and the profession align, agency operates coherently and with greater impact. "In cases where there is agreement among agencies concerning the values, ethical and functional dimensions of agency, we suggest that the overall agency is operating in a zone of moral coherence." Where agencies conflict, the effect of agency is tempered and potentially negated, producing dissonance that may lead designers to question staying in the profession.
requirements: Alignment among the values of designers, clients, organizations and learners
constraints: Designers are at times required to practice outside the zone, causing moral incoherence and dissonance
target_learning_goals: navigating value conflicts in design work
examples: A designer left a position after repeated contradictory supervisor instructions in a rigid, cookie-cutter environment, illustrating moral incoherence
key_sources: The Critical, Relational Practice of Instructional Design in Higher Education: An Emerging Model of Change Agency. (2007). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-007-9061-6

article_title: The learner centric ecology of resources: A framework for using technology to scaffold learning
citation: Rosemary Luckin. (2008). The Learner Centric Ecology of Resources: A Framework for using Technology to Scaffold Learning. Computers & Education 50, 449-462. https://www.veselproject.net
title: ZAA and ZPA as constructs relating the ZPD to educational technology
description: The article defines two constructs that clarify the relationship between the ZPD and educational technology. "The ZAA is used to describe the types of resources, both human and artifact, that are available within a particular context"; the ZPA is "a selected subset of the ZAA that are the resources that are the most appropriate form of assistance for a given learner at a particular moment in time". The article stresses that a rich ZAA alone does not create a ZPD: a more able partner must organise and activate resources, or make existing assistance obvious, so the learner can select appropriately.
requirements: A more able partner must organise and activate the available resources appropriately for the learner to form a ZPA
constraints: The existence of a rich set of resources within the ZAA is not sufficient to ensure the interactions necessary to create a ZPD
target_learners: learners working with more able partners, including teachers, parents and software
target_learning_goals: receiving appropriately challenging activities with the right quantity and quality of assistance
examples: In earlier software scaffolding work the ZAA was within the software, with scaffolding techniques making timely interventions to draw the learner's attention to available assistance, thus creating a ZPA
key_sources: Rosemary Luckin. (2008). The Learner Centric Ecology of Resources: A Framework for using Technology to Scaffold Learning. Computers & Education 50, 449-462. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2007.09.018

article_title: Recommendations for the Investigation and Delivery of Music Programs Aimed at Achieving Psychosocial Wellbeing Benefits in Mainstream Schools
citation: Crooke, A. H. D., & McFerran, K. S. (2014). Recommendations for the investigation and delivery of music programs aimed at achieving psychosocial wellbeing benefits in mainstream schools. Australian Journal of Music Education, 2014(1), 15-37. https://www.asme.edu.au/
title: Two dominant assumptions — that generic music education programs achieve PSWB benefits and that standard quantitative self-report methods can capture them — are unwarranted 'zombie categories'
description: The article identifies two assumptions dominating research and policy: that generic music education programs will facilitate student PSWB, and that quantitative self-report methods are suitable for capturing PSWB benefits. Drawing on critical theory and borrowing from Beck (2002) and Plummer (2011), the authors call these "'zombie categories'" — approaches that are unhelpful in this area and that obscure the reality research aims to uncover, potentially threatening policy support for school music programs.
requirements: Research and policy in this area must be re-designed to avoid relying on these two assumptions when claiming or evaluating PSWB benefits
constraints: The article states its recommendations do not account for all potential challenges nor sufficiently address all those identified
examples: The two studies reported here both used pre-post survey designs dominating the field, and both returned null survey results while interviews reported benefits
key_sources: Crooke, A. H. D., & McFerran, K. S. (2014). Recommendations for the investigation and delivery of music programs aimed at achieving psychosocial wellbeing benefits in mainstream schools. Australian Journal of Music Education, 2014(1), 15-37. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1061963

article_title: The Effect of Using Authentic Task on Teaching Adjectives
citation: Shadi Rastegaran. (2016). The Effect of Using Authentic Task on Teaching Adjectives. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 7(2), 18-24. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.2p.18
title: Zodiac-sign authentic reading texts with dictionary lookup and personal description writing
description: The instructional material evaluated in the study: 12 short printed texts about the 12 zodiac signs, one per session, treated as authentic materials because "everybody has his or her own sign according to their birth month". Learners read each text, looked unknown adjectives up in their dictionaries, and wrote a short description of a classmate or family member born under the same sign using the learned adjectives. The control group instead received dictionary extracts of the same adjectives.
requirements: Target adjectives must be unknown to learners beforehand; known words were omitted from treatment and post-test
constraints: Content is tied to learners' birth months and zodiac signs, a specific authenticity framing
target_learners: Iranian intermediate EFL learners in intact classes
examples: The vocabulary post-test comprised 42 multiple-choice items that were completely unknown to the learners after the pre-test screening
key_sources: Shadi Rastegaran. (2016). The Effect of Using Authentic Task on Teaching Adjectives. Advances in Language and Literary Studies 7(2), 18-24. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.7n.2p.18

article_title: Simultaneous Remote Laparoscopic Training for Trainees Among Multiple Institutions: Can Remote Coaching Replace On-Site Coaching?
citation: Baba Kenji, Hozaka Yuto, Tanabe Kan, Wada Masumi, Kuroshima Naoki, Takara Kinjo, Yoshidome Shizuka, Iio Shunya, Okubo Keishi, Uenosono Yoshikazu, Shimonosono Masakata, Kawasaki Yota, Sasaki Ken, Arigami Takaaki, Ohtsuka Takao. (2024). Simultaneous Remote Laparoscopic Training for Trainees Among Multiple Institutions: Can Remote Coaching Replace On‐Site Coaching? Asian Journal of Endoscopic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1111/ases.70007
title: Simultaneous multi-institution Zoom-based laparoscopic training curriculum with training boxes and real-time remote coaching
description: A three-session curriculum of lectures, practical training, and assessments delivered 1 hour per week, connecting a university hospital and three rural hospitals via Zoom. The article states "all sites were connected via Zoom … for real‐time interactive sessions", with a supervising surgeon giving 15-min lectures and monitoring 30-min practice via an iPad and training box at each facility. A maximum of six trainees trained simultaneously, with no more than two per facility.
requirements: Standard Wi-Fi internet connection at each facility
A training box, an iPad, and laparoscopic instruments and consumable supplies at each facility
At least one senior surgeon present at each facility in case of unexpected situations
constraints: A maximum of six trainees were trained simultaneously, with no more than two participants from each facility
Time available to supervise each participant was limited because multiple facilities trained simultaneously
target_learners: Postgraduate year 1–5 surgical trainees at university and rural hospitals
target_learning_goals: Laparoscopic suture ligation skills, including knot tying and advanced techniques such as overwrapping and running sutures
examples: The first session introduced essential tools and hand-eye coordination, the second covered square, slip, and surgeon's knots, and the third covered overwrapping, wrapping, and running sutures
